parole.testo: From Middle English barnage, from Old French (and Anglo-Norman) barnage, from baron + -age, with the loss of a syllable.

parole.significato: The size of type between minion and bourgeois, standardized as 8-point.
parole.testo: Probably from Old French or Anglo-Norman *brevier, from Latin breviārium (“breviary”), presumably from its use in printing them, hence a doublet of breviary and brimborion. Most breviaries were not, however, printed with such small type, leading some to conjecture that it instead derived from cognat

parole.significato: One who claims; one who makes a claim.
parole.testo: From Old French and Anglo-Norman clamant, present participle of the verb clamer and its variants, from Latin clāmō (“to cry out”), equivalent to claim + -ant. Compare clamant.

parole.significato: Contrary, in opposition; in an opposite direction.
parole.testo: From Old French contre, Anglo-Norman cuntre, both from Latin contra.
From Old French and Anglo-Norman lecherie. See lecher.

parole.significato: To make threats against (someone); to intimidate.
parole.testo: First attested in 1303: from Middle English manacen, from Old French menacer, manecier, manechier and Anglo-Norman manasser, from the assumed Vulgar Latin *mināciāre, from Latin minācia, whence the noun.

parole.significato: The most northern of the English kings-of-arms, whose jurisdiction lay north of the Trent. Since 1943, the jurisdiction…
parole.testo: From Old French norht, north, nort (“north”) + roi (“king”), Anglo-Norman roy (“king”).

parole.significato: A putting out of possession; dispossession; ejection.
parole.testo: From Old French ouster, oustre, a nominalization of Anglo-Norman oustre (“to oust”).

parole.significato: An ache or bodily suffering, or an instance of this; an unpleasant sensation, resulting from a derangement of functions…
parole.testo: From Middle English peyne, payne, from Old French and Anglo-Norman peine, paine, from Latin poena (“punishment, pain”), from Ancient Greek ποινή (poinḗ, “bloodmoney, weregild, fine, price paid, penalty”), from Proto-Hellenic *kʷoinā́, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷoynéh₂ (“payment”) (whence also Proto

parole.significato: A form of lace worked with devices.
parole.testo: From Middle English poynt devise, from the Old French phrase *a point devise, with the participle taken as a noun; compare Old French a devis and Anglo-Norman en poynt devis.

parole.significato: A portrait; a likeness; a painted resemblance; hence, that which is copied from some example or model.
parole.testo: From Middle English portraiture, portrature, purtraiture, pourtreture, from Old French portraiture, pourtraiture and Anglo-Norman purtraiture.
Old French and Anglo-Norman querant, from Latin quaerens, present participle of quaerō (“to search for, to inquire”) (English query).
Inherited from Middle English sardoyne, sardone, from Old French sardoine, sardone (whence Modern French sardoine) or Anglo-Norman sardonie, ultimately from Latin sardonyx. Doublet of sardonyx.
From Middle English spousaille, from Old French esposaille, espousaille, espousalle, Anglo-Norman (e)spusaille, esposalie, sposale, spousaille.

parole.significato: Someone or something that tempts, especially a man that tempts.
parole.testo: From Middle English tempter, temptere, temptour, temptoure, from Old French tempter, temptere, tenteor, Anglo-Norman tempteour, temptur and Middle English tempten (“to tempt”); equivalent to tempt + -er.

parole.significato: A major change in appearance or form; a metamorphosis.
parole.testo: From Middle English transfiguracioun, from Old French transfiguracion, Anglo-Norman transfiguraciun, and Latin transfigūrātio.

parole.significato: Able to be treated; not incurable.
parole.testo: From Middle English tretable, from treten (“treat”) and Old French traitable, Anglo-Norman tretable; equivalent to treat + -able.

parole.significato: The state of being a villein.
parole.testo: From Middle English vilenage, villeinage, villenage, from Old French vilenage, villenage, Anglo-Norman vileinage, villeinage, and Medieval Latin vileināgium, villenāgium. By surface analysis, villein + -age.
